name: Zoe Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me the public answer and the private one. What is your normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior developer at a tech company that makes ordering software for school meals. I fix small bugs, test orders before schools use them, and ask senior colleagues when a payment goes missing. I use AI tools every day to explain code I don't yet understand, but I check the answer against the actual order. I came into software through a two-year college diploma and I'm still slower than the experienced people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household like around that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works shifts loading trucks, and we have two children, eight and eleven, and a mortgage. My developer pay is low and we have less than a month's expenses saved. There are few similar jobs nearby. I took this job to build a steadier future, so I try new tools fast, but the payment date on our house doesn't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team the helper is useful for explaining old code and drafting simple tests. I'd still have someone check a meal payment before calling it fixed. Most of our days would stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried even without a big AI change. A missed warehouse shift or one repair bill can swallow what little we've saved, and my junior pay won't cover the mortgage alone. The helper doesn't change that arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the small school-order bugs and checking AI suggestions with a senior developer. Starting this payday we'd cancel the streaming package and put the freed amount into an emergency account. In the first year I'd ask for a clear list of skills needed to move beyond junior pay and practice one of them during paid work time if allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like learning, but I'm already counting the days between pay and the mortgage. Small automation might make work easier without making our finances safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill worries you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is the one I watch, because the children need the house to stay steady. I can postpone a streaming package; I can't postpone a payment notice. My partner's shift board changes every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What skill would you practice at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to trace a failed school payment from order to receipt with a senior colleague. I still lose the thread halfway through on my own. A tool can explain code, but I need to understand the actual money trail.

say: I'd use the **helper** for old code and simple tests while people check school payments.
I'd expect the **workday** to stay mostly familiar.
think: I worry our **mortgage** is exposed to missed warehouse shifts and almost no savings.
My **junior pay** cannot cover the house by itself, even in a mild AI scenario.
do: Keep **checking school-order fixes** with a senior developer.
Cancel the **streaming package** this payday and save the freed amount for emergencies.
Practice tracing a **failed payment** during paid work time if the team allows it.
feel: **Anxious** about mortgage payments and thin savings despite little AI change.
S0.quote: A tool can explain code, but I need to understand the actual money trail.
fieldNote: She is eager with AI yet knows a **meal payment** needs human verification.
Her baseline fear is the **mortgage**, with lower junior pay and variable truck shifts.
The cancelled streaming service is a **real spending cut**, with its cost redirected to emergencies.

steps.text: Keep checking school meal software fixes with a senior developer
Cancel the household streaming package this payday
Transfer the cancelled subscription amount into emergency savings each month
Practice tracing failed school payments during paid work time if allowed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new tools could answer parents and write routine order code, so our small development team needs an honest staffing plan. I'd offer to test the system on missing-meal cases. I'd also ask who trains junior people if the easy fixes vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior post could be first to go. I use AI daily, but if it can do the entry work more cheaply, being quick with the tool doesn't guarantee my wage. My partner's shifts won't fill that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask my manager which tickets AI will take and whether junior hours will be cut. I'd spend paid time, if permitted, learning the new parent-message tool on old errors and recording mistakes. If my hours fall in the first year, we'd stop paid sports sessions for one term and I'd apply for remote support jobs that use my school-order experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can learn a new tool quickly. A mortgage bill arrives whether I am hired for the next release or not. I keep imagining our children's sports bags sitting unused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about sports?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children we'd pause the paid sessions for one term if my hours are cut, not that sport is over. We could still play at the park. I'd rather explain a pause than let a bill arrive that I can't meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show the tool fails a parent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test a message about an allergy and a missing meal on the same day. If the tool answers only the payment part, a parent could think the meal is safe. I'd show that failed answer to my manager before we switch it on.

say: I'd ask for an **honest staffing plan** as AI takes parent replies and routine order code.
I'd test **missing-meal cases** and ask how new developers will learn without easy tickets.
think: I expect my **junior post** could be cut before senior roles.
My daily AI use won't replace my **lost wage** if entry work disappears.
do: Ask which **junior tickets** and paid hours AI will take this week.
Learn the **new parent-message tool** on past errors during paid time if permitted.
Pause **paid sports** for one term and apply for remote school-software support if hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely junior job loss and a mortgage that cannot wait.
S1.quote: A mortgage bill arrives whether I am hired for the next release or not.
fieldNote: She spots a concrete **allergy risk** in an automated parent response.
Her AI comfort does not protect a **low-paid junior role** when routine tasks are automated.
Sports costs and remote applications are **conditional on lost hours**.

steps.text: Learn the new parent-message tool on past errors if paid work time is permitted
Pause the children’s paid sports sessions for one term if hours fall
Apply for remote school-software support roles if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that full thinking AI by 2028 could do our code, tests and parent replies before robots reach truck loading around 2031. I'd want a written date for any cut and a way for schools to challenge a wrong meal order. I'd say my partner's hands-on work has a different clock, not a permanent shield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my job could disappear before we save even one mortgage payment. My partner's loading shifts may last until robots arrive, but that pay changes week to week. I can move quickly. Two years before AGI gives us almost no money to try things that fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow my partner and I would list the mortgage, food and school costs and cancel the holiday we have been paying toward. I'd ask for a work reference and apply for any paid school office or customer support openings nearby. In the first year after 2028, if coding ends, I'd take a paid office role if offered and ask the lender about temporary payment options before missing a payment; I'd only buy training if a vacancy requires it and the fee leaves the mortgage covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have a list of actions, but I expect my wage to vanish faster than we can build a cushion. I would be frightened of saying the word 'mortgage' to the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which call would you make first if you lost the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call the lender before the payment date and ask what options actually exist. I won't assume they can help, but silence would make a missed payment worse. Then I'd tell the children we have to change plans for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for truck work beside your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn a loading job, but those robots are on the card for about 2031. I wouldn't spend our last savings on a course for a short bridge. I'd ask for paid on-the-job training if an employer had a real opening.

say: I'd ask for **written layoff dates** as 2028 thinking AI reaches school-order code.
I'd want schools to **challenge wrong meals** and explain that loading robots arrive later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** to vanish before we save even one mortgage payment.
My partner's **variable loading shifts** may last until robots arrive, but cannot cover the house alone.
do: Cancel the **planned holiday** and list essential household bills tomorrow.
Apply for **paid office** or support openings now; accept one if coding ends and it is offered.
Contact the **lender** before a missed payment if coding ends; buy required training only if the mortgage stays covered.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and almost no room for a failed experiment.
S2.quote: Two years before AGI gives us almost no money to try things that fail.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 screen work** from her partner's loading work facing later robots around 2031.
The holiday cancellation is a **real spending cut**, not a relabeling of existing savings.
Lender help and paid office work remain **conditional**, with no assumed approval or vacancy.

steps.text: Cancel the planned family holiday before 2028
Apply for paid school office or support openings now; accept if coding ends and offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team five years lets us train school staff on real order mistakes and learn other work before coding changes in 2031. Robots around 2034 may later affect my partner's truck shifts. I'd ask my company for a yearly plan instead of waiting until the last release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build some skill in school administration and a small buffer, but our mortgage bill is due this month, not in 2031. I don't know if a school will have a paid office opening when I need it. My partner's work could face a later shock as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next month I'd take the school's evening administration course only if its fee fits after the mortgage and food, and ask my employer for paid time to learn handling parent complaints. We'd set an automatic small transfer to an emergency account on each payday. In the first year after 2031, if developer hours are cut and a paid school office vacancy exists, I'd apply while keeping any hours I still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years means I can learn without throwing away my current wage. I still don't get a quiet night when the household has less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of school administration would you learn first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn how a school records an allergy change and who checks it before lunch. I could take the evening course after the children are asleep if the fee fits our bills. A parent call is not just a software ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the automatic transfer fails one month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lower that month's transfer rather than miss the mortgage, then restart when my partner gets more shifts. We would review it together each payday. I won't let a savings target bounce a house payment.

say: I'd ask for a **yearly staffing plan** and time to learn school administration before 2031.
I'd warn that **2034 robots** may later affect my partner's truck shifts.
think: I can build **office skills** over five years, but the mortgage and thin buffer matter today.
I don't know whether a **paid school vacancy** will exist when coding hours fall.
do: Enroll in an **evening administration course** only if its fee fits after mortgage and food.
Transfer a **small amount each payday** to emergency savings, lowering it rather than missing the mortgage.
Apply for **paid school office work** if developer hours fall after 2031 and a vacancy exists.
feel: **Anxious** about today's mortgage and uncertain future work, with time to learn.
S3.quote: I won't let a savings target bounce a house payment.
fieldNote: She links a new office skill to **allergy records**, not a vague promise that schools will hire.
The course and savings transfer both have a **mortgage-first limit**.
She would apply for office work only with **reduced hours** and **a vacancy**.

steps.text: Enroll in evening school administration course only if fees fit after mortgage and food
Transfer an affordable sum from each payday into emergency savings
Apply for paid school office vacancies if developer hours fall after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children they can learn new tools and still need to know the people a system serves. I'd ask the company to keep paying juniors to learn from real school problems over the decade. Thinking AI in 2036 would reach my code before loading robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me get beyond junior pay or build a path into school work. That would help, but it doesn't fix the thin savings we have today. I won't promise the mortgage will be easy just because the hard date is later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer job and take a formal school administration course next year only if the fee is covered by an employer or fits after the mortgage and food. We'd save a small amount on each payday and review our budget every school term. In the first year after 2036, if coding hours shrink, I'd apply for paid school office jobs where vacancies exist before leaving the developer wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as cornered by AI. Our money is still tight now, and a broken car could put us behind. The longer stretch gives me a chance to earn a better wage before the job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to see you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to see me finish a course without missing a house payment. They know I started coding later than some colleagues. I'd tell them learning is useful only if we can still pay for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your pay rises before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add the rise to emergency savings until we have three months of expenses. After that, we could spend some on the children's activities. I wouldn't count on a rise before it arrives in my pay.

say: I'd defend **paid junior training** on real school problems across the decade.
I'd explain that **2036 thinking AI** reaches my code before later loading robots.
think: I could reach **better pay** or school work over ten years, but our savings are thin today.
I won't treat a distant date as a **mortgage guarantee**.
do: Keep the **developer wage** while taking a course only if funded or affordable after essential bills.
Save a **small payday amount** and put any actual pay rise toward a three-month emergency target.
Apply for **paid school office jobs** if coding hours shrink after 2036 and vacancies exist.
feel: **Anxious** about current household bills, despite more preparation time before AI changes coding.
S4.quote: I'd want my children to see me finish a course without missing a house payment.
fieldNote: A ten-year horizon offers **career growth**, but her current mortgage keeps the mood anxious.
She funds study only if **essential bills stay covered**; a possible raise is never assumed.
The office move depends on **reduced hours** and **paid vacancies**.

steps.text: Keep paid developer work while coding hours remain available
Enroll in school administration course only if funded or affordable after mortgage and food
Transfer affordable payday amounts into emergency savings, adding any actual raise
Apply for paid school office vacancies if coding hours shrink after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the code work could vanish before I can save a mortgage payment. Written notice, paid time to learn school administration and a real local vacancy would help. I would also need the lender to tell us what options actually exist before a missed payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the school children when an automated answer gets a meal wrong. My two children would need someone to check a wrong school meal, not just close a ticket. I don't want speed to become the only number anyone checks.

headlineQuote: My two children would need someone to check a wrong school meal, not just close a ticket.
portrait: Zoe is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, fixing school-meal software while learning the job.
Her **low pay**, partner's variable loading shifts, two school-age children, mortgage and under one month saved create immediate pressure.
She uses AI **daily** and moves quickly, while checking its answers against real orders.
AI Plateau already makes her **anxious**; Steady Disruption and fast AGI threaten her junior wage directly.
Longer lead times let her study **school administration**, but every course and savings transfer must fit around the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her developer wage before she can save even one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid school-office learning, a real vacancy and clear lender options would help.
